Tribe
TRīB
n. (rendering Hebrew shebet and matteh, Greek phulē)
From Latin tribus, one of the three original divisions of the Roman people. The Hebrew words are more vivid than the English: shebet and matteh both mean a rod, staff, or sceptre, and both came to mean a tribe — the branch that springs from one stock, and the staff that marks a chieftain's authority. When Aaron's rod budded among the twelve rods of the tribes, the pun was the point: the tribe is the rod. Greek phulē is from phuō, to grow or spring up, and carries the same image of a stock branching.

Biblical Definition

A tribe in Scripture is a household grown into a nation without ceasing to be a household, and the twelve are treated as a fixed and God-given order rather than an accident of descent: “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them; every one according to his blessing he blessed them” (Gen 49:28). The blessings are prophecies, and each tribe's history unfolds along the line Jacob laid down. The tribes are not merely a census category but the shape of worship, going up together to one place: “Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the LORD” (Psa 122:4) — unity without uniformity, twelve distinct companies with one destination and one Name. The whole arrangement narrows at last to a single tribe and a single Person, for the sceptre was promised to Judah and the promise is claimed in heaven: “behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof” (Rev 5:5). And the category is then opened outward rather than abolished, for the redeemed are numbered not as an undifferentiated mass but as a great multitude “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) standing before the throne. Distinction of peoples survives redemption; what does not survive is division and enmity between them.

Webster 1828 Definition

A family, race, or division of a people descended from one ancestor; specifically one of the twelve divisions of Israel descended from the sons of Jacob; and in Revelation the tribe of Judah from which Christ sprang and the tribes and tongues of the redeemed.

expand to see more

TRIBE, n. 1. A family, race, or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor and kept distinct.

2. A division, class, or distinct portion of a people, whether from the same or different ancestors; as the twelve tribes of Israel.

3. In Hebrew, a rod, staff, or sceptre; hence the branch springing from one stock, and the authority borne over it.

4. A number of things having certain characters in common; a class or order.

5. In Scripture, whither the tribes go up. Psalm 122. The Lion of the tribe of Juda. Rev. 5.

Key Scripture

Genesis 49:28 — "All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them; every one according to his blessing he blessed them."

Psalm 122:4 — "Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the LORD."

Revelation 5:5 — "And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof."

Revelation 7:9 — "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number , of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;"

Modern Corruption

Ethnic and cultural identity is absolutised into the fundamental category of human standing, so that men are classed first by group and judged accordingly — a framework Scripture answers with one-in-Adam and one-in-Christ.

expand to see more

The modern tribalism that treats group identity as the deepest fact about a person is not the Bible's doctrine of tribes but its inversion. Scripture's anthropology has two universal terms and they are both about standing before God, not standing among men: all are one in Adam, in whom all sinned and die, and the redeemed are one in Christ, in whom there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free. Any framework which makes an inherited group the ground of guilt or of innocence has replaced the categories Scripture actually uses — sin, the fallen heart, covenant faithfulness and covenant breaking — with a category the gospel was given to dissolve. The point is not that ancestry is nothing; it is that ancestry cannot bear the weight of ultimate judgment, and the attempt to make it do so produces the very enmity it claims to cure.

The opposite error is a flattening universalism which supposes that because we are one in Christ, all particular belonging is now suspect — that family, people, and nation are obstacles to be transcended. The last book of the Bible refuses this too. The redeemed multitude is described precisely by nations and kindreds and people and tongues (Rev 7:9); the distinctions are still legible in glory. What is abolished is the wall of partition and the enmity, not the diversity. The principle to recover is that the gospel does not erase the tribes but reconciles them, and that a church which loses either half — the real unity or the real particularity — has ceased to picture what John saw before the throne.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shebet and matteh both mean a rod, staff, or sceptre, and by extension a tribe — the branch from one stock under one authority. Greek phulē, from phuō to spring up, is a tribe or clan.

expand to see more

Hebrew shebet (H7626) — rod, staff, sceptre, tribe; the sceptre shall not depart from Judah (Gen 49:10) uses the same word as the tribes themselves.

Hebrew matteh (H4294) — a staff, rod, or branch, and hence a tribe; the twelve rods of Num 17, one for each tribal house, of which Aaron's budded.

Greek phulē (G5443) — a tribe or clan, from phuō, to grow or spring forth; used of the twelve tribes and of the tribes of the earth.

Greek patria (G3965) — a lineage or family descending from a father; rendered kindred in Rev 7:9 and family in Eph 3:15.

Hebrew shebet Yehudah — the tribe of Judah, the royal tribe of the promised sceptre, whence the Lion of the tribe of Juda (Rev 5:5).

Usage
